docs.title: Hi, I'm LaMeisha DuBose
docs.text: Senior GRC professional building toward a future where compliance isn't a checklist. It's infrastructure.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm a Senior GRC professional based in New York, building at the intersection of cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, and AI governance. My background is in enterprise risk management, SOX ITGC, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and audit readiness — I've spent my career learning how governance programs actually work inside fast-moving technology organizations, and more importantly, where they break down.

What I'm working toward is the engineering side of that problem: translating policy into infrastructure, generating evidence artifacts automatically, and building continuous monitoring systems that catch drift in real time — not during the next annual audit. The goal isn't point-in-time compliance. It's compliance that runs.

docs.title: Currently working on
docs.text: The GRC Engineering Challenge — a 6-week public build where each week adds one layer to the same compliance system. By week 6: compliant infrastructure as code, a policy library, a CI gate, signed evidence, native cloud controls, and a full OSCAL control mapping.

docs.title: Reference templates
docs.text:
Three fill-in-the-blank starting points for GRC documentation — a policy, a risk assessment, and a control mapping. Skip straight to whichever you need.

Don't need these?

These are optional. To remove them: delete docs/templates.md, then remove the Templates line from the nav: section in mkdocs.yml.

  • Policy template
  • Risk assessment template
  • Control mapping template

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: What risk or requirement does this policy exist to address? One or two sentences.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Who and what systems does this policy apply to? Be specific — "all production AWS accounts," not "the cloud."

docs.title: Policy statement
docs.text: The actual rule. Write it the way it would be tested in an audit — clear enough that a control owner can't misread it.

docs.title: Roles & responsibilities
docs.text: Role Responsibility Policy Owner Control Owner Reviewer

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text: How is this policy technically or procedurally enforced? Link to the automation or process, not just the intent.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: Process for requesting and approving exceptions, and who signs off.

docs.title: Review cycle
docs.text: How often is this reviewed, and by whom. (e.g., "Annually, or upon material change to scope.")

docs.title: Related controls
docs.text: Map this to the frameworks it satisfies — SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIST CSF, etc.

docs.title: Asset description
docs.text: What is being assessed — the system, data flow, or process. Include what data it touches and where it lives.

docs.title: Threat scenarios
docs.text:
# Threat Likelihood (1-5) Impact (1-5) Risk Score Notes 1 2 3

Scoring key: Risk Score = Likelihood × Impact. 1-6 = Low, 7-14 = Medium, 15-25 = High.

docs.title: Existing controls
docs.text: What's already in place that reduces likelihood or impact for each threat above?

docs.title: Residual risk
docs.text: After existing controls, what's left? This is the number that should drive the remediation plan.

docs.title: Remediation plan
docs.text: Action Owner Target Date Status

docs.title: Sign-off
docs.text: Who reviewed and accepted this assessment, and when.

docs.title: Control mapping template
docs.text: Maps one control across the frameworks you're tracking, so you can show — not just claim — cross-framework fluency.

docs.title: Control description
docs.text: What is this control actually doing? Written in plain language before you map it to any framework's jargon.

docs.title: Framework mapping
docs.text: Framework Control ID Control Language SOC 2 ISO 27001 NIST CSF PCI DSS

docs.title: Evidence type
docs.text: What counts as proof this control is operating — a screenshot, a config export, a log query result, an approval trail.

docs.title: Testing frequency
docs.text: How often is this control tested, and is that testing manual or automated?

docs.title: Gaps identified
docs.text: Where do the frameworks disagree, or where does your current evidence fall short of what an auditor would expect?

docs.title: Project 01 (Example): Automating Quarterly Access Reviews with Okta Access Certifications
docs.text: This is a filled-out example, included so you can see what "recruiter-ready" actually looks like before you write your own. Delete this file (or move it to a /examples folder) once you've built your first real one — don't ship someone else's project as your own.

docs.title: The Compliance Gap
docs.text: Quarterly user access reviews were done manually — pulling access lists, emailing managers, chasing sign-offs in spreadsheets. No consistent evidence trail, and every cycle ate days that could have gone into actual risk work.

docs.title: The Scope & Assumptions
docs.text: All active Okta-managed applications and their assigned users. Assumes Okta is the identity source of truth for in-scope systems — access managed outside Okta (break-glass accounts, local admin) is out of scope and handled through a separate process.

docs.title: The Engineering Solution
docs.text: Built recurring access certification campaigns in Okta Access Certifications, routed to the correct resource owners automatically, with reviewers required to explicitly approve or revoke each access grant instead of a blanket sign-off. Replaced the manual spreadsheet cycle entirely.

docs.title: Auditor-Ready Evidence
docs.text:
Campaign: Q_Access_Review
Status: Completed
Reviewers: 12
Access grants reviewed: 340
Revoked: 18
Completion time: 15 seconds (system-generated certification report,
vs. ~3 weeks for the prior manual process)

(Replace with your own exported certification report or screenshot when you build your real version.)

docs.title: The Security Impact
docs.text: Reduced access review turnaround from roughly 3 weeks to same-day, with a clean, timestamped evidence trail an auditor can pull directly instead of reconstructing from email threads. The time recovered went straight into risk management work — this project is what started the shift from GRC analyst to GRC engineer.

docs.title: Project 01: [Name Your Project]
docs.text: This is where you turn a manual GRC process into proof of engineering skill. Hiring managers scan for structure, not just code. Fill out every section below — a blank one is a red flag, not a shortcut.

docs.title: The Compliance Gap
docs.text:
What was actually broken or missing? Name the control and the framework it maps to.

Example: "The organization lacked daily proof that MFA was active, violating SOC 2 CC6.1."

docs.title: The Scope & Assumptions
docs.text:
What's in scope, what's explicitly out of scope, and what you assumed going in.

Example: "AWS production account, targeting all IAM users. Assumes root account MFA is out of scope — handled separately."

docs.title: The Engineering Solution
docs.text:
What you actually built. Name the tools. This is the part that proves you can execute, not just describe.

Example: "Built a serverless continuous monitoring pipeline using AWS Config, Lambda, and EventBridge."

docs.title: Auditor-Ready Evidence
docs.text:
Paste the real output — JSON, Terraform plan, S3 verification log, screenshot. This is the receipt. Redact anything sensitive before it goes public.

[Paste your evidence output here]

docs.title: The Security Impact
docs.text:
The before/after in numbers. This is the line a recruiter will actually remember.

Example: "Reduced audit prep from 3 weeks to 15 seconds."
